analysis.title: There Is No Free Boom!
key_insights: Citadel Securities' Nohshad Shah says the Fed delivered its first hike since 2023 last week, and the market path has moved from roughly four cuts priced in April 2025 to almost five hikes including September's move.

September composite PMI rose to 58.4, the strongest reading in more than five years, with broad-based gains in activity, employment and new orders. S&P Global says the survey is consistent with annualised growth of about 5%, in line with the Atlanta Fed GDPNow tracking at 5%.
Input-cost inflation in the September PMI jumped to its highest level since October 2022 as strong demand met supply constraints and rising energy costs.

Shah argues fiscal policy, not monetary policy, is now the primary driver of the US economy. Procyclical fiscal easing into an economy near capacity has kept growth stronger and inflation and rates higher for longer.
CBO projects a $1.9tn deficit (5.8% of GDP) this year, with federal debt held by the public rising from 101% of GDP to 120% by 2036.

One Fed hike cannot offset years of fiscal expansion. 10y Treasuries pushed above 5.10% and 30y above 5.40% despite the hike, because the bond market is pricing how much nominal demand and duration it must absorb.

The US is both the main source of the higher global discount rate and better placed to absorb it. France and the UK face similar borrowing-cost increases with weaker growth, more exposure to the energy shock and no AI-investment offset. France faces a debt-sustainability problem and the UK looks more like stagflation.

Microsoft 365 Copilot has more than 30mn paid seats against an estimated 250-300mn enterprise knowledge-worker base, about 10% penetration. Shah sees a capability overhang where diffusion of existing models could support years of inference growth.

Shah is unconvinced that falling token prices are bearish for compute. Agents turn one instruction into a persistent workflow of repeated model calls, so cheaper tokens expand the addressable market and widen the winner set from accelerators to CPUs, memory, storage, networking and cybersecurity. He remains bullish on the compute complex.

China may deploy AI better through the physical economy: it accounted for 54% of global industrial-robot installations in 2024, operates over two million factory robots, and Beijing targets above 90% adoption of next-generation intelligent terminals and agents by 2030.

BloombergNEF's base case has China adding almost six times as much power-generation capacity as the US over the next five years, while the US is constrained by grid connections, permitting and local opposition to data centres.

Shah criticises the AI industry's safety messaging, arguing that framing job loss or existential risk undermines public support for the land, power and permits needed to build AI infrastructure. He backs Jensen Huang's standard of not releasing systems that cannot be contained and shown to be under control.

sector_views.rationale: Falling token prices expand compute demand, broadening winners from accelerators to CPUs, memory, storage, networking and cybersecurity.

macro_indicators.reading: First hike since 2023 delivered in September; market path equivalent to almost five hikes including September's move
macro_indicators.interpretation: The Fed has moved to tightening, but fiscal policy keeps growth and inflation high, so Shah sees rates higher for longer.
Strongest reading in more than five years, consistent with roughly 5% annualised growth.
Tracking growth in line with the PMI-implied pace.
Strong demand colliding with supply constraints and rising energy costs points to sticky inflation.
Yields rose despite the Fed hike, reflecting fiscal supply and duration demands.
Long-end yields are structurally higher on fiscal issuance.
Deficits remain historically large with unemployment below 5%, which Shah calls procyclical easing.

macro_indicators.indicator: US federal debt held by the public (CBO)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Rising debt adds to duration supply and the interest bill.

risk_factors: Fiscal deficits and issuance keep inflation and long-term yields higher for longer.
Input-cost inflation is rising as demand meets supply constraints and higher energy costs.
France faces debt-sustainability risk and the UK stagflation risk as the global discount rate rises.
US grid connections, permitting and local opposition to data centres constrain AI power supply.
Public backlash tied to AI job-loss and existential-risk messaging could raise the cost of power and permits and bring blunt regulation.
Persistent AI agents that hold credentials and take real-world actions pose engineering safety risks.
geopolitical: US-China AI race: the US leads in frontier models while China may lead in deployment through factories, robots and power capacity.
Rising energy costs and an energy shock are cited as pressure on Europe, especially France and the UK.
Shah says US-China safety cooperation on incident reporting is possible but technology détente is not.

tension_points.bull_case: Fiscal policy and the AI capex boom support US demand, investment and returns on capital. September composite PMI is 58.4 and GDPNow tracks about 5%, giving the US a growth cushion.
tension_points.bear_case: The same forces keep inflation sticky and yields structurally higher. 10y is above 5.10% and 30y above 5.40% despite the Fed hike, and one hike cannot offset years of fiscal expansion.

tension_points.theme: Falling token prices and compute demand
tension_points.bull_case: Cheaper tokens make more agent workflows economically viable, expanding compute demand and broadening winners across CPUs, memory, storage, networking and cybersecurity.
tension_points.bear_case: Falling price per unit of intelligence could shrink compute demand, a view Shah says he is unconvinced by.

theme_stances.evidence: fiscal policy remains in the driving seat

theme_stances.evidence: America develops the better models…but China has more places to run it
